acoustic.note: Gas turbine ships are louder than diesel-electric types, and the towed array and bow sonar make her an active participant in the underwater fight.

visual.note: A 154 m grey hull with a tall deckhouse is easy to see on a clear day, but it shows a low profile from a distance.

brief.whatItIs: The Flight II Arleigh Burke is a 154 m US Navy guided-missile destroyer. It carries the Aegis combat system, whose four fixed radar arrays track hundreds of air targets at once and steer long-range Standard missiles onto them. USS Mahan was the first Flight II ship and is the example used here.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander uses it as the air-defence anchor of a task group. It sits between the carrier or the convoy and the threat axis and keeps the SPY-1D radar on full power so incoming aircraft and missiles are picked up early. The Standard missiles, which need the three SPG-62 illuminators in the final seconds, are the main reach. Harpoon missiles give it an anti-ship punch of its own, and the 5-inch gun and Phalanx deal with small boats and leakers. Its weakness is magazine depth: the 90 vertical cells hold only so many missiles, and a swarm of cheap boats or drones can burn them faster than the ship can reload at sea. Mahan fired warning shots at IRGC boats in the Strait of Hormuz in January 2017, which is the kind of close encounter the ship's guns and lookouts are for.
typicalMissions: Air and missile defence of a carrier or convoy
Anti-surface warfare and maritime security patrol
Anti-submarine escort with towed array and helicopter
Presence and escort in the Strait of Hormuz

brief.whatItIs: The Flight IIA is the most common version of the Arleigh Burke destroyer. It adds two helicopter hangars at the stern, so the ship carries its own helicopters instead of only landing them. The SPY-1D(V) radar and Aegis combat system are the same family as Flight II. USS Mustin (DDG 89) is the example ship.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander uses it the same way as a Flight II: as an air-defence escort that stays on the threat side of the carrier or convoy with the SPY-1D(V) radar on. The hangars change the picture below the surface and over the horizon. Two MH-60R helicopters give it a second set of eyes against submarines and small boats, and they can carry anti-submarine torpedoes and Hellfire missiles. Standard missiles handle aircraft and missiles at long range, ESSM adds close-in air defence, and Tomahawk gives land strike. The weakness is the same as any destroyer: the vertical launch cells are the magazine and cannot be reloaded quickly at sea. Treat the missile counts in this record as typical, not fixed.
typicalMissions: Air and missile defence of a carrier or convoy

brief.whatItIs: The Bayandor class is a 1960s patrol frigate design, built in Texas as the US 'PF 103' type and handed straight to Iran. At 84 m and about 1,135 tons it is one of the larger Iranian ships still active before the 2026 war. It carries a 76 mm gun, a twin 40 mm gun and light cannon. A 2013 refit is reported to have added two twin Noor anti-ship missile launchers; the Sandkasten engine entry keeps the original gun-only fit.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander uses this ship as a gun-armed escort and presence vessel, not a front-line fighter. It can run anti-piracy patrols, shadow merchant traffic and add a gun and a lookout to a group of faster boats. Its 76 mm gun is useful against small craft out to a few kilometres, but its radar and electronics are dated, and it has no real anti-air missiles. Against a modern warship or aircraft it is easy to find and slow at 20 knots. Keep it behind other defences and use it to extend the picture of the sea around Iranian waters, not to take on warships.

records.className: Northrop Grumman E-2 Hawkeye, E-2C Hawkeye 2000 version
records.role: Carrier-based airborne early warning and command-and-control aircraft

serviceWindow.statusNotes: The Hawkeye 2000 configuration first deployed in 2003 with VAW-117 aboard USS Nimitz. The US Navy has largely replaced its E-2Cs with the E-2D Advanced Hawkeye, so the Navy's own front line is now E-2D. The E-2C still serves with other nations, including Egypt, France, Japan, Taiwan and Mexico. The retired field is left open because the E-2C family as a whole remains in service.

dimensions.crew: 5 (pilot, copilot, combat information center officer, air control officer, radar operator)

records.propulsionSummary: Two Allison T56-A-427 turboprops of 5,100 equivalent shaft horsepower each turn eight-blade NP2000 propellers.

sensors.role: 360 degree airborne early warning radar in the rotating dome, tracking air and surface targets and passing them to the fleet. The Hawkeye 2000's published detection range is greater than 640 km (400 mi).

sensors.name: AN/ALR-73 passive detection system
sensors.role: Passive receiver that detects and locates enemy radar emissions without transmitting. No public detection range found, so this is an open estimate.

loadouts.name: Airborne early warning station
loadouts.role: Fly an orbit about 175 nautical miles from the carrier and watch the air picture; the aircraft carries no weapons. The Northrop Grumman sheet gives about 4 hours 24 minutes on station at that distance.

radar.note: A large twin turboprop with a 7 m rotodome and no stealth shaping gives a big radar return.

infrared.note: Two turboprops give a modest heat signature compared with a jet fighter.

acoustic.note: Large propellers make it loud and easy to hear from the ground or the sea surface.

visual.note: A 24.5 m wingspan and the large rotodome make it easy to see.

brief.whatItIs: The E-2C Hawkeye 2000 is a twin-engine turboprop that takes off from an aircraft carrier carrying a large rotating radar dome on its back. It sees much farther than a ship's radar because it flies high. The crew of five direct fighters and warn the fleet of incoming aircraft and missiles.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander sends the Hawkeye up ahead of the carrier group to cover the likely approach direction. It stays on a long orbit, tracks everything in the air and over the sea, and hands targets to fighters and ships through data links. Link its picture to the ships so their missiles can engage targets beyond their own radar. The aircraft is unarmed and slow, so it needs fighter cover and must be kept away from enemy long-range air-to-air missiles. Its radar and its radio links are strong signals the enemy can detect, which is the trade-off for its range. If it is lost, the group loses most of its early warning.

visual.note: A large airframe about 19 m long with a wide wing span when unswept, easy to see against the sky.

brief.whatItIs: The F-14D Tomcat was the last and best version of the US Navy's big swing-wing fleet defence fighter. It had a pilot and a radar officer, stronger F110 engines than earlier models, and a newer radar. It was built to protect a carrier group by shooting down enemy bombers from far away. The Navy retired the whole F-14 fleet in 2006, so in this scenario it is a what-if aircraft.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander used the Tomcat as the outer layer of carrier defence. Pairs flew combat air patrols out along the likely approach path of enemy aircraft, with the radar officer tracking many targets at once and the pilot firing the long-range AIM-54 Phoenix missile when targets were still beyond 100 nautical miles. The wings sweep back for speed and forward for slow carrier landings and long loiter time. Its strengths are radar reach, missile range and the number of targets it can engage together. Its weaknesses are a large radar and infrared signature, high fuel burn and heavy maintenance demands. Enemy fighters with their own long-range missiles, or a lack of tanker support, can cut its effective reach sharply.

brief.whatItIs: The F/A-18E Super Hornet is the US Navy's main carrier-based fighter. It is a single-seat, twin-engine jet that can shoot down other aircraft and also bomb ground targets or sink ships on the same sortie. It is a larger, longer-ranged development of the older F/A-18 Hornet.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander keeps Super Hornets on deck as a flexible striking arm. In the air they fly escort for strike packages and patrol stations around the carrier group, using the AESA radar to see air targets far out and fire AMRAAM missiles before the enemy gets close. For a sea-control mission, two to four aircraft carry Harpoon anti-ship missiles and attack ships from beyond the range of most shipboard air defence. The aircraft is fast and agile but it is a conventional airframe, so its radar and infrared signatures are real. A pair flying low over open water stays hard to catch for an enemy with only gun or short-range defences, while a modern surface-to-air missile ship will still find it. Tanker aircraft and the carrier itself decide how far it can reach.

records.designation: Boghammar Marin RL-118 / RL-130-4A high-speed patrol boat

serviceWindow.statusNotes: Iran bought about 50 from the Swedish yard Boghammar Marin AB, ordered in 1983 or 1984 depending on the source, and the Guards were using them by February 1987. The International Institute for Strategic Studies estimated about 40 still operational in 2020. The boats are over 40 years old and the Guards also use newer Iranian-built speedboats, so how many Boghammars were fit on 2026-03-15 is uncertain. (Sources s1, s3, s6.)

brief.whatItIs: The Boghammar is a 12.8 m aluminium-hulled speedboat that the Swedish firm Boghammar Marin built as a pilot and patrol boat. Iran bought about 50 in the 1980s and fitted them with machine guns, rocket launchers and recoilless rifles. The Revolutionary Guard Navy used them in the Tanker War of 1987 and 1988 and still uses them today. They are tiny and can go about 45 knots.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander uses Boghammars in swarms of a dozen or more. The idea is to overwhelm a warship's gun and radar by coming from several directions at once, and to hit lightly protected targets like tankers and supply ships with machine guns and rockets. One boat carries a machine gun and a rocket launcher, so it can hurt a small ship but it cannot sink a destroyer. Its weakness is the same as its strength: it is small and open, so a helicopter gun, a 30 mm or 57 mm naval gun, or a single rocket will destroy it. In the 1988 battle with US forces, Boghammars were hit and sunk by attack aircraft. Use them from behind islands and inside shipping lanes, and pull them back once US helicopters arrive.

brief.whatItIs: The F-14A Tomcat is a large two-seat American swing-wing fighter built to shoot down bombers at long range with the AIM-54 Phoenix missile. Iran is the only country besides the United States to have flown it. Iran received about 79 aircraft before 1979 and has kept some flying for decades with improvised repairs and parts from outside the usual supply chain.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander in this scenario would treat the Iranian Tomcat as a high-value but fragile asset. In good condition the AWG-9 radar can detect large aircraft far out and a Phoenix can reach beyond 100 nautical miles, so a single pair can force an opponent to respect a long barrier line. In practice, spare parts are scarce, Phoenix stocks are short, and radar and engine reliability is poor. Iranian pilots are more likely to fly short defensive patrols close to ground radars than long deep strikes. A US fighter with an AESA radar can usually detect and engage a Tomcat first, so the Iranian side gains most when it keeps aircraft hidden and uses them for a surprise shot. The number available on any given day is small and uncertain.
typicalMissions: Long-range interception of strike aircraft and patrol aircraft

brief.whatItIs: The F-4E Phantom II is a big twin-engine American jet from the 1960s that served as both a fighter and a bomber. It carries a pilot and a weapons officer, an internal 20 mm cannon, and a heavy load of missiles and bombs. Iran bought a large fleet in the 1970s and still flies a shrinking number of them today.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander in this scenario would use Iranian Phantoms as a low-end strike and patrol force, not as a front-line air defence fighter. Their radar is old and range is limited, so they work best near friendly ground radars and against targets that cannot shoot back well. They can fly low over water to attack ships and boats with Maverick missiles or unguided weapons. Against a modern US Navy fighter with an AESA radar and AMRAAM missiles, a Phantom is outranged and easy to detect. Spare parts are scarce, so sortie rates are low and a commander should expect many aircraft to be unavailable on any given day.

brief.whatItIs: The Kaman class is a set of 47 m missile boats that France built for Iran in the 1970s (the La Combattante II design). Iran swapped their original Harpoon missiles for Chinese-type C-802 (Noor) missiles around 2000. Each boat carries four missiles, a 76 mm gun forward and a 40 mm gun aft. They are small, fast and cheap, but old.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander uses these boats as a coastal missile threat: with four C-802 missiles reaching about 120 km they can threaten a warship that is nowhere near the boat's own radar range, if someone else supplies the targeting. They work best in small groups that fire together from near the coast and break away at 35 knots. The 76 mm gun is a decent weapon against small boats, but the boats have almost no protection against missiles or aircraft: a few chaff launchers and a few light guns. They sink with one or two hits. Their age makes mechanical failures likely, so expect fewer boats to be ready than the roster says.

brief.whatItIs: The Nimitz class is the US Navy's workhorse aircraft carrier. USS Nimitz, the lead ship, is 333 m long, displaces about 97,000 tons and carries an air wing of about 85 aircraft: strike fighters, early-warning aircraft, electronic attack jets and helicopters. Two nuclear reactors give it effectively unlimited range.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander uses the carrier as a mobile airbase and the centre of a strike group. The air wing does the fighting: fighters shoot down aircraft, strike aircraft hit ships and shore targets, and the E-2 early-warning aircraft sees farther than any ship radar. The carrier itself carries only close-in defences (Sea Sparrow, Phalanx, chaff and an electronic warfare suite), so cruisers and destroyers must ring it and carry the long-range air and missile defence. It can launch about four aircraft a minute from its four catapults. Its weakness is that a hit on the flight deck or hangar can stop air operations, and if the carrier is damaged the whole group loses its main weapon. Keep it away from submarines and out of reach of saturating missile salvos.

acoustic.note: Gas turbines on a single shaft; it is not a quiet platform for a submarine to listen to, and it tows its own array to hear them first.

visual.note: A 138 m ship is easy to see at sea in daylight.

brief.whatItIs: The Oliver Hazard Perry class was the US Navy's mass-produced guided-missile frigate from the late 1970s. The long-hull version, such as USS Taylor, is 138 m long and carries two SH-60B helicopters in a hangar. It was built to escort convoys and carrier groups against submarines and aircraft at a low cost per ship.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander uses a Perry as a picket and escort. The SPS-49 radar watches the air picture, the sonar and towed array listen for submarines, and the two SH-60B helicopters extend the ship's reach out past the horizon in both anti-submarine and surface search. The single Mk 13 launcher holds 36 SM-1 Standard missiles and 4 Harpoon missiles in one shared magazine, so it can fire only one missile at a time and the load runs out fast against a big raid. The Phalanx gun is the last-ditch defense against sea-skimming missiles. Keep it inside a larger group's air cover when facing heavy air threats. Its low-mounted ESM and limited missile magazine are the weak points.

infrared.note: Four turboprops give a moderate heat signature, much lower than a jet airliner of this size.

acoustic.note: Four large propellers are loud, but a submerged submarine usually cannot hear an aircraft flying overhead.

visual.note: A 30 m wingspan and a long fuselage are easy to spot, especially at the low altitudes used for sonobuoy drops.

brief.whatItIs: The P-3C Orion is a four-engine turboprop patrol aircraft flown from land bases. It stays in the air for many hours to hunt submarines and watch the sea surface. It carries sonobuoys, a radar, an infrared camera, radar warning gear and a magnetic detector, with torpedoes and missiles for attack. The Update III is the version fitted with the improved acoustic computer system.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander sends the Orion out to cover a large patch of ocean for hours, flying low for sonobuoy drops and higher for radar search. It drops patterns of sonobuoys, listens for a submarine, uses the magnetic detector to pin it down and attacks with a torpedo. Against surface ships it uses radar and infrared to find and identify them, and can fire Harpoon or Maverick missiles. It is slow and has no defenses against fighters or surface-to-air missiles, so keep it clear of enemy air cover. Its strength is long endurance and an effective sonobuoy search. Its weakness is that it needs a friendly air base within a few hundred miles.
typicalMissions: Maritime patrol and surface ship surveillance

records.name: SH-60B Seahawk
records.role: Ship-based anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare helicopter (LAMPS Mk III)

serviceWindow.statusNotes: The SH-60B went operational in 1984 and the US Navy retired it on 11 May 2015, replacing it with the MH-60R. The wider SH-60 family continues in US and allied service in other versions. In the 2026 scenario this is a legacy airframe, kept as the helicopter that Perry-class frigates carried; the Navy itself now flies the MH-60R.

records.propulsionSummary: Two General Electric T700-GE-401C turboshaft engines, rated at roughly 1,700 to 1,900 shaft horsepower each depending on the source, drive a single four-blade main rotor.

sensors.name: AN/APS-124 search radar
sensors.role: Surface search under the nose; finds ships and surfaced submarines and relays the picture to the parent ship. No public detection range found, so this is an open estimate matching the engine value.

sensors.name: AN/ALQ-142 ESM
sensors.role: Passive radar warning and emitter bearing. No public range found, so this is an open estimate.

sensors.name: Sonobuoys (25-tube launcher) and towed MAD
sensors.role: Air-dropped passive and active sonobuoys listen for submarines and a towed magnetic anomaly detector confirms metal below. Both work only at short range. No public range found, so this is an open estimate.

sensors.name: Optional nose-mounted FLIR turret
sensors.role: Thermal camera for identifying surface contacts. No public range found, so this is an open estimate.

loadouts.name: LAMPS Mk III anti-submarine patrol
loadouts.role: Find and attack submarines ahead of the parent ship using sonobuoys and up to two lightweight torpedoes

loadouts.name: LAMPS Mk III surface patrol
loadouts.role: Radar search and attack against small surface ships with the Hellfire missile, with the Penguin missile as another option and a cabin-door gun for close work

radar.note: A helicopter of this size has a small radar return, but its rotor blades give strong Doppler returns when it hovers.

infrared.note: Two turboshaft engines with exposed exhaust give a clear heat source; an infrared jammer is on some Seahawk versions.

acoustic.note: Rotors make a loud, recognisable noise, and it flies low and slow when it hovers to dip or drop sonobuoys.

visual.note: A 20 m dark helicopter is small but visible at low level in daylight.

brief.whatItIs: The SH-60B Seahawk is the US Navy helicopter built for the LAMPS Mk III system. It lives in the hangar of a frigate, destroyer or cruiser and flies out to find submarines and small ships beyond the ship's own radar horizon. It carries a search radar, sonobuoys, a towed magnetic detector and lightweight torpedoes.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander launches it to extend the parent ship's eyes by 100 nautical miles or more. In an anti-submarine role it flies a search pattern, drops sonobuoys to listen and then attacks with a torpedo once the target is located. In a surface role it uses radar to see ships, passes the contact to the parent ship and can attack small boats with Hellfire missiles. It is slow, carries little fuel (about 4 hours of mission time) and has no defenses beyond decoys, so keep it away from active fighters and surface-to-air missiles. Its biggest strength is giving a small ship a second set of sensors.
typicalMissions: Anti-submarine search ahead of a ship or convoy
Attack on small surface craft with Hellfire missiles
Search and rescue and vertical replenishment

records.name: Sina-class fast attack craft

serviceWindow.statusNotes: First boat (Paykan) commissioned September 2003; Iran planned about ten, and only five to six had been completed by the mid-2020s. Most hulls were built and based in the Caspian Sea (Bandar Anzali), with Zereh at Bandar Abbas from 2021, so only a few are Gulf-based. Wikipedia reports Sina-class boats were destroyed in strikes during the 2026 war, including two Caspian boats on 18 March 2026, which is three days after the scenario date of 2026-03-15; how many were still afloat and fit on 2026-03-15 is not reliably published. (Sources s1, s5.)

records.propulsionSummary: Diesel engines driving propeller shafts for about 35 knots; GlobalSecurity says the Sina uses Chinese diesels, and the exact engine model and power are not published in the sources used.

weapons.name: C-802 Noor
weapons.mountSummary: Four missiles in box launchers amidships; Iran's Noor is a copy of the Chinese C-802. Range 120 km, Mach 0.9 cruise (595 kts) and the 165 kg warhead are the published C-802 figures (s4); 165 kg gives 165 damage points at 1 point/kg. Pk is the METHODS.md table.

weapons.name: 23mm ZU-23-2
weapons.mountSummary: The boat's light-gun fit approximated as a twin 23 mm: published Sina fits list a 76 mm gun, a 40 mm gun and two 12.7 mm machine guns, while the Chinese-built Tondar (Houdong) boats the old label refers to carry ZU-23-2. Effective range 2.5 km is published (s6); 200 rounds is our estimate. Pk and 23 mm damage are the METHODS.md table.

sensors.name: Surface search radar (masthead radome)
sensors.role: Detects ships and low aircraft for the gun and missile targeting

sensors.name: Fire-control radar and optical director
sensors.role: Aims the 76 mm gun

sensors.name: Bridge lookouts and binoculars
sensors.role: Spotting small craft and surface contacts by eye

radar.note: A 47 m hull of about 300 tons with a compact low superstructure; much smaller than any frigate.

infrared.note: Diesel exhausts at high speed are hot, though a small boat is hard to pick out at long range.

acoustic.note: Fast diesel boat with high-speed propeller noise; not built for quiet running.

visual.note: Low, grey hull that sits close to the water.

brief.whatItIs: The Sina class is a 47 m missile boat that Iran built at home. It is an updated copy of the French Combattante II design that Iran bought for the Shah's navy (the Kaman class), and the first boat entered service in 2003. Each carries four C-802 type anti-ship missiles (Iran calls its copy Noor) and a 76 mm gun. Older Sandkasten data labels this entry [Houdong], which is wrong: the Houdong is a separate Chinese-built boat that Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy calls the Tondar class.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander uses this boat as a carrier for four long-range missiles: the 120 km reach of the C-802 lets it hit a ship from well outside its gun range. The boat's own radar sees only a few dozen kilometres, so the best results come when a coastal radar, drone or helicopter feeds it a target. The usual play is to launch from behind an island or from coastal clutter and then run for port. It has no anti-air missiles, only a 76 mm gun and light cannon, so a couple of hits from any warship will sink it. Keep it in port or in a protected group until the strike moment, and do not leave it in open water where helicopters and strike aircraft can find it.
typicalMissions: Anti-ship missile strike from the coast
Escort and screening for Iranian convoys
Show-of-force presence in Caspian and Gulf waters

records.name: Ticonderoga-class cruiser (Baseline 3)
records.role: Aegis guided-missile cruiser for air defence, surface warfare, anti-submarine warfare and land strike

serviceWindow.statusNotes: The example ship, USS Bunker Hill (CG 52), was commissioned on 20 September 1986 and decommissioned in September 2023 (s4). The class is not gone: the Navy is keeping USS Gettysburg (CG 64), USS Chosin (CG 65) and USS Cape St. George (CG 71) in service on extended service lives running through fiscal year 2029 (s5). A small number of other Ticonderoga hulls were still in service on 2026-03-15; this record does not state an exact count because no source fetched for it gives one. The class entry stays active for that reason.

records.propulsionSummary: Four General Electric LM2500 gas turbines drive two shafts for about 80,000 shaft horsepower.

weapons.name: RIM-66M SM-2MR
weapons.mountSummary: Fired from the Mk 41 vertical launch system (FAS notes vertical launchers from CG 52 on; 122 cells); missile count is a typical mix, not a published load. Range 167 km is the Navy fact file's 'up to 90 nautical miles' (s15); speed 2,316 kts is the published Mach 3.5 (4,290 km/h, s18). The Mk 125 warhead's mass is not published; 100 kg is our estimate (about 14% of the published 707 kg launch mass, s18), giving 100 damage points at 1 point/kg. Pk is the METHODS.md table.

weapons.name: RGM-84 Harpoon
weapons.mountSummary: Two quad launchers (8 missiles). Range 124 km is the Navy fact file's 'over 67 nautical miles' (s14); speed 467 kts is the published 864 km/h (s19). Warhead 221 kg (published, s19) gives 170 damage points (1 point/kg, capped at 170). Pk is the METHODS.md table.

weapons.name: Mk 15 Phalanx CIWS
weapons.mountSummary: 20 mm six-barrel gun; the class carries two mounts, the engine models one. 1,550-round magazine and 4,500 rounds/min are published (s20). Range 1.5 km is the published 1,486 m maximum effective range (s20). Pk and 20 mm damage are the METHODS.md table.

sensors.name: AN/SPY-1A phased-array radar
sensors.role: Aegis air search and track, four fixed arrays, FAS says it tracks air contacts beyond 200 miles

sensors.name: AN/SPS-49 air search radar
sensors.role: Long-range 2D air search that backs up the SPY-1 on ships that keep it, picks out low-radar-cross-section targets in clutter and jamming

sensors.name: AN/SPS-55 surface search radar
sensors.role: Surface search and navigation

sensors.name: AN/SPG-62 fire control radars
sensors.role: Illuminates the target for semi-active SM-2 missiles in the last seconds of flight

sensors.name: AN/SQS-53 bow sonar
sensors.role: Hull-mounted active and passive search for submarines

sensors.name: AN/SQR-19 towed array
sensors.role: Passive long-range listening for submarines on a cable towed behind the ship

sensors.name: AN/SLQ-32 electronic support
sensors.role: Detects, identifies and bears on hostile radars

sensors.name: Bridge and lookout watch
sensors.role: Eyes and binoculars from the bridge and weather decks

radar.note: A 173 m hull with a tall, boxy superstructure and two large masts. It was built on the Spruance hull before radar cross-section shaping became a design goal.

infrared.note: Four gas turbines put out a strong exhaust plume, the same as on a destroyer.

acoustic.note: Gas turbine ship of about 9,600 tons. Active bow sonar adds a deliberate noise source when it pings.

visual.note: A large grey ship with a tall deckhouse and two stacks is easy to spot.

brief.whatItIs: The Ticonderoga class is the US Navy's cruiser: a 173 m Aegis warship built on the Spruance destroyer hull with a larger missile battery and more command space than a destroyer. USS Bunker Hill (CG 52) was the first ship with vertical launchers. She was decommissioned in September 2023, but the class is not retired.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander uses a cruiser as the air-defence coordinator for a carrier group or a surface action group. The SPY-1A radar and the older SPS-49 search radar build the air picture, and the Aegis system hands targets to Standard missiles. Tomahawk missiles give it strike reach on land, and the 5-inch guns and Phalanx cover small boats and leakers. The extra command space lets a flag officer run the air defence of the whole group from this ship. Its weak points are age and magazine depth. The hulls are close to 40 years old, so material readiness varies from ship to ship, and the missile cells cannot be reloaded quickly at sea. Treat the missile counts in this record as typical.
typicalMissions: Air defence coordination for a carrier strike group
Anti-submarine escort with towed array and helicopters
